sources.title: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed.
sources.locator: Author-hosted full PDF downloaded and inspected. Chapter 5 §§5.1, 5.3–5.4 (printed pp. 102–118): parameterized priors, full hyperparameter posterior, normal random-effects mean squares, method-of-moments estimates, and point-estimate plug-in limitations. Chapter 7 §7.4 (printed pp. 182–184): model posterior odds, Bayes factors, proper marginal densities, point hypotheses, prior sensitivity, and improper-prior comparison.

contents.name: §5.1 Constructing a parameterized prior distribution
contents.support: The section identifies empirical Bayes as a point estimate of prior hyperparameters, explains that it ignores posterior uncertainty, and contrasts it with a full joint Bayesian model.

contents.name: §5.3 Joint, conditional, and marginal posterior distributions
contents.support: The section derives the full joint posterior and its hyperparameter marginal by integration, supporting the distinction between retaining a hyperparameter posterior and fixing a point estimate.

contents.name: §5.4 Normal model with exchangeable parameters: balanced ANOVA expected mean squares
contents.support: The balanced normal random-effects ANOVA table gives expected between and within mean squares sigma squared plus n tau squared and sigma squared.

contents.name: §5.4 Difficulty with a natural non-Bayesian estimate of the hyperparameters
contents.support: The section solves the two expected-mean-square equations to obtain the raw variance-component moment estimate (MSB-MSW)/n.

contents.name: §5.4 Plugging in point estimates and interpreting a negative variance estimate
contents.support: The text says the raw estimate can be negative and that replacing it by zero can overstate the claim that the group means are identical.

contents.name: §5.4 Full posterior over hyperparameters versus a point-estimate plug-in
contents.support: The section says substituting point estimates ignores uncertainty in the unknown hyperparameters, while the full model retains their posterior distribution.

contents.name: §7.4 Model comparison using Bayes factors
contents.support: The displayed model-odds identity is prior odds multiplied by the ratio of the two model-specific integrated marginal densities, which are defined only when proper.

contents.name: §7.4 Continuous-model prior sensitivity and improper-prior comparison
contents.support: The normal-prior variance example shows the Bayes factor depends strongly on prior spread; the flat improper-prior comparison is not defined without a normalization convention.

contents.name: §7.4 Discrete model comparison with proper marginal densities
contents.support: The book distinguishes a scientifically discrete point hypothesis with a proper model marginal from a point inside a continuous parameter family.

sources.title: Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 8, Posterior Inference & Prediction
sources.locator: Full official HTML chapter inspected. §§8.2.1–8.2.2, lines 92–188: posterior and prior odds, the odds-ratio definition of a Bayes factor, exact point nulls under a continuous prior, and the interval-buffer alternative.

contents.name: §8.2.1 One-sided tests and prior/posterior odds
contents.support: The text defines a Bayes factor as posterior odds divided by prior odds, matching the finite-model theorem's odds identity.

contents.name: Bayes Factor
contents.support: The theorem locally proves that the evidence ratio equals posterior odds divided by prior odds.

contents.name: §8.2.2 Two-sided tests and a point null under a continuous parameter
contents.support: The chapter explicitly computes zero prior and posterior probability at an exact point under a continuous prior and notes that the resulting odds are undefined.

contents.name: §8.2.2 Buffering a point null by a nonzero interval
contents.reason: This pair preserves the exact point-null model-atom example; it does not introduce interval-null hypotheses or posterior-probability testing for interval alternatives.

contents.name: §8.2.1 No universal Bayes-factor cutoff
contents.support: The Definition remarks that a Bayes factor is an odds multiplier and supplies no universal cutoff that decides which model is true.

sources.title: Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 16, (Normal) Hierarchical Models without Predictors
sources.locator: Full official HTML chapter inspected. §16.3.1 and §§16.4.1–16.4.3: the within-group, between-group, and global-prior layers, posterior simulation retaining global parameters, and group-specific posterior summaries.

contents.name: §16.3.1 The hierarchy
contents.support: The hierarchy has group-level sampling, group-parameter distributions indexed by shared global parameters, and priors on those global parameters.

contents.name: §16.4.1 Posterior simulation
contents.support: The posterior simulation first draws global parameters from their posterior and then draws group parameters conditionally, retaining uncertainty in the shared layer.

contents.name: §16.4.2 Posterior analysis of global parameters
contents.support: The global hyperparameters remain posterior-distributed and are shared across groups; the example locally proves that integrating a shared parameter can make group parameters dependent.

contents.name: §16.4.3 Posterior analysis of group-specific parameters
contents.support: Group-specific posterior quantities are formed together with the global parameter draws, supporting the full-posterior versus fixed-hyperparameter contrast.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, §7.4.4, What are variance components?
sources.locator: Full official page inspected, lines 9–47: random-effects interpretation, the one-way ANOVA table and expected mean squares, method-of-moments equations, negative estimates, and REML as an alternative.

contents.name: 7.4.4 Random-effects model and ANOVA expected mean squares
contents.support: The balanced example has EMS sigma_epsilon squared plus r sigma_tau squared for between groups and sigma_epsilon squared for within groups, under independent Gaussian random effects and errors.

contents.name: Method of moments estimates of variance components
contents.support: The handbook equates the expected and observed mean squares and solves for the raw variance-component estimate.

contents.name: Negative method-of-moments variance-component estimate
contents.support: The handbook states the method-of-moments estimate can be negative and recommends considering alternatives; the local example shows a positive-probability negative-estimate region even when the true variance is positive.

contents.name: Restricted maximum likelihood alternative
contents.reason: The assigned design establishes the ANOVA moment equations and their negative-estimate warning, but does not develop REML estimation or its confidence intervals.
